questions.stem: An insurance operations team wants Claude to pull five fields (policy number, claimant name, incident date, loss type and estimated amount) out of first-notice-of-loss emails. The fields are well defined, and the team already has 300 labelled emails for testing. A consultant proposes spending two weeks writing 30 hand-crafted few-shot examples before running anything. The team lead wants the approach that reaches a reliable result with the LEAST wasted effort. What should the architect recommend?

options.text: Write the 30 examples first, because few-shot prompting reliably beats zero-shot prompting on extraction tasks and the examples will be needed anyway.
Skip prompting work and move straight to the most capable model, since a stronger model removes the need for examples or careful instructions.
Ask Claude to rate its own confidence in each extracted field and treat the low-confidence fields as the signal for which examples to write later.
Start with a clear zero-shot prompt defining each field and its format, run it on the 300 labelled emails, and add examples only for the failures found.

questions.explanation: With clear field definitions and a labelled test set already available, the efficient path is to **measure first**. A clear, direct zero-shot prompt is a sensible baseline, and running it against the 300 emails shows exactly where it fails (date formats, missing amounts, multi-claim emails). Examples are one of the most reliable ways to steer output, so add them where the eval shows a gap, and choose them to cover those specific failure cases. That spends effort where evidence says it is needed rather than up front.

whyWrong.A: Few-shot often helps, but it is not automatically required, and 30 examples written blind may miss the real failure modes while adding tokens to every request. Anthropic suggests 3 to 5 relevant, diverse examples, not 30, and without a baseline you cannot tell whether they helped.
whyWrong.B: A larger model raises cost and latency without addressing unclear instructions, and it still has not been measured against the labelled set.
whyWrong.C: Self-reported confidence is not a reliable error signal. The team already has ground-truth labels that show real failures directly.

questions.mindset: Baseline with clear zero-shot instructions and a real eval set, then add examples where the data shows failures.

questions.stem: A tax-advisory product uses Claude with thinking enabled to analyse unusual cross-border situations. To make reasoning "more rigorous", an engineer added a 25-step hand-written procedure to the prompt that Claude must follow in order on every case. Since then, results on routine cases are unchanged, but on novel cases that don't fit the procedure, answers have become worse: Claude forces the facts through steps that don't apply. What change is MOST likely to restore quality on novel cases?

options.text: Replace the rigid procedure with high-level guidance to think thoroughly about the rules and the facts, keep the criteria the answer must satisfy, and re-run the evals.
Extend the procedure with additional steps covering each novel case seen so far, so that every future situation maps onto a defined step in the sequence.
Ask Claude to re-check its final answer against the 25-step procedure after it finishes, so any step it skipped gets applied before the response is returned.
Turn thinking off and require the full step-by-step reasoning to appear in the visible answer, so reviewers can see exactly where the procedure went wrong on each case.

questions.explanation: Anthropic's guidance for thinking says to **prefer general instructions over prescriptive steps**: a prompt like "think thoroughly" often produces better reasoning than a hand-written plan, because Claude's reasoning frequently exceeds what a human would prescribe. The symptom (worse on cases the procedure didn't anticipate) is exactly what an over-prescriptive plan causes. Keeping the success criteria while freeing the method, then confirming on the eval set, addresses the cause.

whyWrong.B: Growing the procedure makes it more rigid and will always lag the next unanticipated case. It doubles down on the cause of the regression.
whyWrong.C: A self-check against the same rigid procedure reinforces the problem: it pushes answers back toward steps that don't apply.
whyWrong.D: Turning off thinking removes the model's built-in reasoning, and visible reasoning does not fix the forced-fit behaviour. On current models a prompt that demands the reasoning be written out in the response can also be declined (a reasoning-extraction refusal). It trades quality for transparency that wasn't the problem.

questions.mindset: With thinking on, give goals and criteria, not a hand-scripted method; over-prescription hurts novel cases.

questions.stem: A logistics pricing service runs in a configuration where the model's built-in thinking is turned off for latency reasons. Quotes involve multi-step arithmetic (weight tiers, surcharges, discounts), and accuracy improved noticeably once the prompt asked Claude to work through the calculation before answering. However, the downstream service now fails because it expects a single number and receives paragraphs of working. What is the MOST reliable fix that keeps the accuracy gain?

options.text: Remove the instruction to work through the calculation, because the parser needs a single number and the reasoning text is what is breaking the integration.
Keep the step-by-step instruction, ask Claude to put only the final amount inside <answer> tags, and have the service extract just the tag contents.
Ask Claude to reason silently in its head and print only the final number, so the working stays private and the output stays a single number.
Post-process the response with a regular expression that takes the last number appearing anywhere in the text and passes it to the service.

questions.explanation: When thinking is off, Anthropic documents manual chain-of-thought as the fallback: ask Claude to think through the problem before answering and **put the final answer in `<answer>` tags so you can extract it**. Separating the reasoning from the answer keeps the accuracy benefit of visible working and gives the parser a clean, deterministic target. (On models where thinking is available, relying on built-in thinking at a suitable effort level is the preferred route.)

whyWrong.A: This throws away the step that produced the accuracy gain. The integration problem is about separating output, not about the reasoning itself.
whyWrong.C: Without thinking enabled, "reason silently" gives no space to reason. Asking for only the number is effectively the zero-shot setup that was less accurate.
whyWrong.D: "Last number in the text" is fragile: the working may end with an intermediate value, a unit or a date. A tagged answer is an explicit contract.

questions.mindset: Separate reasoning from the answer with tags so you keep CoT accuracy and get a parseable result.

questions.stem: A revenue-recognition assistant uses Claude with thinking enabled to classify complex contracts under the company's accounting policy. Reviewers find that Claude reaches the right category on simple contracts but on bundled deals it often uses a method the controllers reject: it judges the contract as a whole instead of first separating the distinct obligations. The controllers have five previously resolved bundled deals with documented reasoning. Which change MOST directly teaches Claude the approach they expect?

options.text: Add the five resolved deals as examples that show only the contract text and the final category, so Claude learns which category each type of bundle maps to.
Raise the effort level to the maximum for every contract, so that Claude spends more thinking on bundled deals and is more likely to notice the separate obligations.
Add the five deals as tagged worked examples, each showing the contract, the method applied (identify each obligation, then classify) and the expected answer.
Add a capitalised rule at the top of the prompt saying Claude MUST NEVER classify a bundled contract as a whole, with a warning that violations are critical errors.

questions.explanation: Anthropic notes that **multishot examples work with thinking**: worked examples shape how Claude approaches similar problems in its own thinking, and they are best presented as *problem, method, expected answer*. The failure here is the method, not the label, so examples that show the controllers' method (split into obligations first) are the most direct lever. Wrapping them in example tags keeps them distinct from instructions.

whyWrong.A: Input-to-label examples teach the outcome, not the method. Claude may memorise surface mappings without learning to split obligations on new deals.
whyWrong.B: More thinking does not tell Claude which method the controllers accept. It adds cost on every contract and may still apply the rejected approach more thoroughly.
whyWrong.D: A negative, shouty rule says what not to do without showing what to do, and aggressive language can cause over-application on contracts where whole-contract treatment is correct.

questions.mindset: When the method is wrong, show the method: worked examples (problem, method, answer) steer thinking.

questions.stem: A pharmaceutical company uses Claude to draft patient-information leaflets. Today one large prompt asks Claude to write the draft, check it against 14 readability and regulatory criteria, and return a corrected version. Quality is acceptable, but the regulatory affairs team must now show auditors, for each leaflet, which criteria the draft failed and what was changed. Which design BEST meets the new requirement while maintaining quality?

options.text: Keep the single prompt and ask Claude to append a short note at the end of each leaflet listing the criteria it believes the final version satisfies.
Keep the single prompt but enable the highest effort level, so the internal review is more thorough and fewer of the 14 criteria are missed.
Have a human reviewer rewrite every leaflet against the 14 criteria and record the changes, using Claude only to format the reviewer's approved text.
Split the work into separate calls: draft, review against the 14 criteria with structured findings, then revise from those findings, logging each step.

questions.explanation: Anthropic describes **prompt chaining** as still useful when you need to *inspect intermediate outputs or enforce a specific pipeline structure*, and names self-correction (draft, review against criteria, refine) as the most common pattern, with each step a separate call that you can log, evaluate or branch on. The auditors need the intermediate review, so it must exist as its own logged artefact rather than being hidden inside one response.

whyWrong.A: A self-reported note about the final version doesn't record which criteria the *draft* failed or what changed. It is also unverifiable after the fact.
whyWrong.B: Higher effort may improve the internal check, but it produces no separate, auditable record of findings and changes.
whyWrong.C: This discards the working automation to meet a traceability need that a chained pipeline meets directly. It is costly and slow.

questions.mindset: Chain prompts when intermediate results must be inspected, logged or audited.

questions.stem: A customer-success manager with no engineering background built a prompt that drafts replies to customer emails. After the instructions she pasted two approved sample exchanges (a customer email followed by the ideal reply), separated from the instructions and from the real customer's email only by blank lines. The tone of the drafts is good, but in some runs Claude answers the question asked in one of the samples instead of the real customer's question, and occasionally addresses the real customer by a sample customer's name. What is the BEST fix?

options.text: Wrap each sample in its own example tag inside an examples block, and put the real customer's email in a separately labelled tag, so instructions, examples and input are clearly delimited.
Add a sentence after the samples telling Claude that they are only illustrations and that it must respond to the most recent customer email rather than to any sample.
Remove the two samples and expand the instructions into a longer description of the desired tone and structure, since the samples are what the model is confusing with the real email.
Move to a more capable model, which is better at working out from context which of several emails in a prompt is the one that actually needs a reply.

questions.explanation: Anthropic's guidance says examples should be **structured**: wrap them in `<example>` tags (several inside `<examples>`) so Claude can **distinguish them from instructions** and from the real input. Here nothing marks where the samples end and the live email begins, so Claude sometimes treats a sample as the task. Tagging the examples and the input removes the ambiguity at its source while keeping the tone benefits the samples provide.

whyWrong.B: A disclaimer leaves the prompt structurally ambiguous: Claude still has to guess where the samples end and the live email starts. Clear structure is more reliable than an instruction about unclear structure.
whyWrong.C: Examples are one of the most reliable ways to steer tone and format, and a longer prose description tends to be less consistent. The problem is the missing boundaries, not the use of examples.
whyWrong.D: A bigger model costs more and still receives an undelimited prompt. The fix is structural, cheap and lives in the prompt.

questions.mindset: Delimit examples and inputs with tags so Claude can tell instructions, examples and the real task apart.

questions.stem: A bank routes customer complaints into "service", "product" and "regulatory". Regulatory complaints must reach a specialist team within 24 hours. The prompt says "be careful to flag anything that might be regulatory". Evals show two problems: many plain service complaints are flagged regulatory, and some genuine regulatory complaints worded casually are missed. Which TWO changes are MOST likely to improve both precision and recall? Choose TWO.

options.text: Change the instruction to "only flag regulatory if you are very confident", so Claude stops over-flagging ordinary service complaints.
Replace the vague instruction with explicit criteria for what makes a complaint regulatory, such as alleged mis-selling or data misuse, plus what does not.
Ask Claude to output a confidence percentage with each label and route anything above 50% to the regulatory specialist team.
Switch to the largest available model so that it understands financial regulation in more depth than the current model does.
Add tagged examples of borderline cases: casually worded complaints that are regulatory and alarming-sounding ones that are not, with the reason.

questions.explanation: The prompt's guidance is vague, so Claude guesses where the boundary lies. Anthropic's core advice is to **be clear and direct**, and examples are among the most reliable ways to steer behaviour. Explicit categorical criteria define the boundary, and **diverse examples that cover edge cases** show how to apply it to tricky wording in both directions. Together they target both false positives and false negatives.

whyWrong.A: Swapping one vague threshold for another moves errors from false positives to false negatives. More regulatory complaints would be missed, which is the costlier failure.
whyWrong.C: Self-reported percentages are not calibrated probabilities, and a 50% cut-off adds a number without defining what regulatory means.
whyWrong.D: The failures come from an undefined boundary, not missing knowledge. A larger model given the same vague instruction still has to guess.

questions.mindset: Replace 'be careful' with explicit criteria and boundary examples.

questions.stem: A legal operations manager with no engineering background is building a prompt that summarises NDAs into a fixed one-page format. She has only two approved summaries to use as examples, both for short mutual NDAs. Early tests on long one-way NDAs drift from the format. She asks how to build a better example set quickly without lowering quality. Which TWO approaches should the architect recommend? Choose TWO.

options.text: Ask Claude to propose additional example summaries covering other NDA types, then have a lawyer correct and approve them before they go into the prompt.
Paste in 25 more summaries of short mutual NDAs from the archive, because a larger example set produces more consistent formatting than a small one.
Pick test documents where the format drifted, such as long one-way NDAs, and turn approved summaries of them into examples so the set covers those cases.
Let Claude generate and insert new examples automatically on each run, so the example set keeps adapting without anyone reviewing it.
Remove the two examples and describe the one-page format in a longer paragraph, since examples that don't match every case confuse the model.

questions.explanation: Anthropic's tips say to include **3 to 5 relevant, diverse examples** and that you can **ask Claude to generate additional examples** from an initial set or evaluate existing ones for relevance and diversity. Generating candidates and having a lawyer approve them scales the set safely. Drawing examples from the cases where output drifted makes the set cover real edge cases instead of more of the same.

whyWrong.B: More of the same kind of example adds tokens but not coverage. The drift is on long one-way NDAs, which none of these represent.
whyWrong.D: Unreviewed, changing examples remove quality control and make results inconsistent between runs. Examples steer output strongly, so they need approval.
whyWrong.E: Examples are one of the most reliable ways to steer format. The issue is that the two examples lack variety, not that examples are used at all.

questions.mindset: Grow few-shot sets for coverage, not volume; Claude can draft candidates, and a human approves them.

questions.stem: A platform team uses a Claude coding agent to write data-transformation functions. Each task comes with a suite of unit tests, but the agent can only read and write files. About a fifth of submitted functions fail the tests in CI because of edge-case bugs the agent never noticed. Which change is MOST effective at catching these errors before submission?

options.text: Add several examples of well-written transformation functions to the prompt so the agent sees the coding style that tends to pass tests.
Add an instruction asking the agent to be extremely careful with edge cases and to review its function mentally before submitting it.
Give the agent a tool that runs the test suite and instruct it to verify its function against the tests and fix failures before it finishes.
Generate three candidate functions per task at higher effort and submit the one the agent itself judges to be the most robust.

questions.explanation: Anthropic recommends asking Claude to **self-check against concrete test criteria** before finishing, and, for long autonomous tasks, **providing verification tools** so Claude can confirm correctness without continuous human feedback. The tests already exist; letting the agent run them turns self-checking from a hopeful re-read into an objective signal it can act on.

whyWrong.A: Style examples don't reveal the specific edge-case bugs in a given function. The failures need a feedback signal, not more patterns.
whyWrong.B: "Be careful" and a mental review have no objective signal. The agent already believed its functions were correct.
whyWrong.D: Three candidates triple cost, and picking one by the model's own judgement still never runs the tests that define correctness.

questions.mindset: Self-checking works when the model can verify against real criteria, so give it the tool to run them.

questions.stem: A credit-operations agent calls an `approve_limit_change` tool. To create an audit trail, an engineer added a required `step_by_step_reasoning` parameter whose description asks Claude to write out its full chain of thought for the decision. After deployment, some requests end in refusals related to reasoning extraction, and the audit team still needs a justification for every call. What should the architect do?

options.text: Keep the parameter but mark it optional, so that Claude can leave it empty whenever it declines to fill it in and the tool call still goes through.
Replace it with a parameter asking for a short explanation of the decision and its supporting evidence, leaving the reasoning itself in thinking.
Force the tool call with tool choice settings so that Claude can't decline, and keep the full chain-of-thought parameter required.
Move the chain-of-thought request into the system prompt and ask Claude to repeat its complete reasoning verbatim in every tool call.

questions.explanation: Anthropic's tool-definition guidance says: **ask for an explanation, not reasoning**. If a parameter asks why Claude is making the call, request a short explanation or the supporting evidence; a parameter that asks for the model's thinking or step-by-step reasoning may lead to a `reasoning_extraction` refusal. A concise justification with evidence is also a better audit record than a long reasoning dump.

whyWrong.A: Making it optional loses the justification the audit team needs on exactly the calls that trigger the problem, and the parameter still asks for the wrong thing.
whyWrong.C: Forcing tool use doesn't change what the parameter asks for, so the reasoning request that triggers the refusal is still there. Forced tool choice is also not supported on every model and thinking setting, so it is a fragile lever to build an audit trail on.
whyWrong.D: Moving the same request into the system prompt still asks Claude to expose its reasoning, so it doesn't remove the cause.

questions.mindset: Ask for a justification and evidence in outputs; keep reasoning in thinking.

questions.stem: A lender's covenant-monitoring tool sends Claude one 180-page loan agreement at a time, placed above the analyst's question. Answers are usually right, but analysts complain that some answers paraphrase loosely and occasionally rely on a clause that turns out to concern a different facility. They want answers that stay grounded in the actual text, with the least added infrastructure. What should the architect change?

options.text: Split the agreement into five equal sections and send five separate requests, then concatenate the five partial answers into one response.
Move the question above the agreement so Claude knows what to look for before it reads the long document text.
Add an instruction to answer only when very confident and otherwise reply that the agreement is unclear on the point.
Ask Claude to first extract the word-for-word passages relevant to the question in quote tags, then answer using only those quotes.

questions.explanation: For long documents, Anthropic recommends **grounding responses in quotes**: ask Claude to extract the relevant parts first, then carry out the task based on them. This focuses Claude on the relevant content, and the quotes let analysts check which clause an answer relies on. The document is already above the question, which is the recommended order, so the remaining fix is quote-first grounding.

whyWrong.A: Fixed splits can separate a definition from the clause that uses it, and stitching partial answers can produce contradictions. It also adds orchestration.
whyWrong.B: Long documents work best at the top with the query at the end. Moving the question first goes against the guidance and can reduce quality.
whyWrong.C: A vague confidence rule doesn't tie answers to text. It may increase non-answers without stopping loose paraphrase.

questions.mindset: For long documents, extract quotes first, then answer from them.

questions.stem: A software company's support assistant answers product questions from a 600,000-token knowledge base. Because the chosen model has a 1M-token context window, an engineer proposes sending the whole knowledge base with every question "so nothing is ever missing". Typical questions need two or three articles. What is the BEST response to the proposal?

options.text: Retrieve only the articles relevant to each question and send those, because accuracy degrades as context grows and the full base adds cost on every call.
Accept the proposal, since fitting inside the context window means the model will reliably find the right article in every request.
Accept the proposal but cache the knowledge base as a stable prompt prefix, so the 600,000 tokens are cheap to reuse and the cost objection disappears.
Summarise the whole knowledge base into one 50,000-token digest and send that digest with every question instead of the articles.

questions.explanation: Anthropic's context-window docs warn that **more context isn't automatically better**: as token count grows, accuracy and recall degrade (*context rot*), so curating what's in context matters as much as available space. Sending 600k tokens to answer from two or three articles also multiplies input cost and latency on every request. Retrieving the relevant articles keeps context focused and cheap.

whyWrong.B: Fitting in the window is not the same as being used well. Recall degrades with context size, and the cost is paid on every question.
whyWrong.C: Caching lowers the price of the repeated prefix, but the 600,000 tokens still occupy the context window on every call and recall still degrades with context size. It addresses cost, not the accuracy problem.
whyWrong.D: A digest loses the exact details (steps, settings, versions) that support answers need, while still adding a large fixed cost to every call.

questions.mindset: A big context window is capacity, not a strategy; curate what goes in.

questions.stem: A team enables thinking on its report-generation service to improve analysis quality. They left `max_tokens` at the value sized for the old reports. Shortly afterwards, many reports arrive cut off mid-sentence, and the responses show `stop_reason: "max_tokens"`. The input is well within the context window. What is the MOST likely cause and fix?

options.text: Thinking tokens count toward the context window but not toward max_tokens, so the input must be trimmed to make room for the reports.
The model is refusing part of each report, so the team should rephrase the instructions and retry the truncated requests.
Thinking tokens are part of max_tokens, so thinking now uses up the output budget; raise max_tokens and handle the max_tokens stop reason.
The output was cut off by rate limits, so the team should add retries with exponential backoff until the full reports arrive.

questions.explanation: Anthropic's docs state that **thinking tokens are a subset of `max_tokens`** and are billed as output. With the old `max_tokens`, thinking now consumes much of the budget, leaving too little for the report, so generation stops with `max_tokens`. The fix is to size `max_tokens` for thinking plus output and to handle the `max_tokens` stop reason explicitly rather than shipping truncated reports.

whyWrong.A: This reverses the rule: thinking does count toward `max_tokens`. The input is well within the window, so trimming it doesn't address the cap.
whyWrong.B: A refusal shows as `stop_reason: "refusal"`, not `max_tokens`. Rewording won't help when the budget is the limit.
whyWrong.D: Rate limits return 429 errors; they don't produce successful responses that stop with `max_tokens`.

questions.mindset: Thinking spends from the same max_tokens budget as the answer, so resize it when you enable thinking.

questions.stem: A market-research agent investigates a question by reading 150 to 200 web pages and filings. All raw page content flows into the single agent's context. Late in each run, the agent repeats searches it already did and the final synthesis ignores findings from early sources. Cost per run is also rising. Which architecture change BEST addresses both quality and token use?

options.text: Move to a model with a larger context window so that every page fits comfortably in a single run and nothing has to be dropped before the synthesis.
Have a lead agent delegate source groups to subagents that read in their own context and return condensed, cited findings for the lead to synthesise.
Instruct the agent to read each page more carefully and to keep a running list of earlier findings in its replies so it doesn't repeat searches.
Raise the effort level for the whole run so the agent reasons harder about which sources it has already covered and what still remains to be read.

questions.explanation: Anthropic's context-engineering guidance describes **sub-agent architectures**: specialised subagents explore with clean context windows and return condensed, distilled summaries, so the lead agent's context holds findings rather than raw pages. This tackles context rot (lost early findings, repeated searches) and keeps the lead's token load small. The detailed search context stays isolated in the subagents.

whyWrong.A: A bigger window lets more raw text pile up, but recall still degrades as context grows and cost rises with every token.
whyWrong.C: A "mental list" lives in the same overloaded context. Instructions can't overcome the structural problem of too much raw content.
whyWrong.D: More reasoning effort raises cost and doesn't reduce the raw content crowding the context.

questions.mindset: Isolate exploration in subagents and pass back distilled results, not raw material.

questions.stem: A field-service assistant uses server-side compaction for long troubleshooting conversations. The default summaries were dropping part numbers, so an engineer supplied a custom summarisation prompt that says only "Preserve every part number and serial number mentioned." Part numbers now survive, but after compaction the assistant forgets which fixes were already tried and what the technician's goal was. What is the MOST likely cause and fix?

options.text: Compaction is running too early in each conversation, so the trigger threshold should be raised so that the history is summarised less often.
Compaction is losing context that summaries cannot reliably keep, so it should be turned off and the full history sent on every turn instead.
The model needs more effort after compaction, so effort should be raised on the turns that immediately follow each summary block.
A custom summarisation prompt replaces the default one, so it must describe everything to keep, including the goal, steps tried and open items.

questions.explanation: Anthropic's compaction docs say that custom summarisation `instructions` **replace the default prompt entirely**; they don't supplement it. The default prompt is written for continuity (state, next steps, learnings), and the one-line replacement told Claude to keep identifiers and nothing else, so the goal and attempted fixes were no longer preserved. The fix is a complete prompt that lists every category the conversation needs to continue: the goal, actions taken and their results, open questions, and the exact identifiers. (For values that must survive exactly, a structured facts block kept outside the summarised history is a further safeguard.)

whyWrong.A: Delaying compaction postpones the loss but doesn't change what the summary keeps. The next summary would drop the same context.
whyWrong.B: Sending the full history gives up the reason for compaction: context limits and quality degradation as conversations grow.
whyWrong.C: Effort can't restore information that the summary never captured.

questions.mindset: A custom summary prompt replaces the default, so specify everything the next turn needs.

questions.stem: A product manager notices that a research assistant began failing with "prompt is too long" errors on very long sessions. An engineer replies that this can't be a context problem because the large reference pack at the start of every request is prompt-cached. What should the architect explain?

options.text: Caching changes what those tokens cost, not whether they count: cached tokens still occupy the window, so the session needs context management.
The cache has expired between turns, and once the reference pack is written to the cache again it will stop counting toward the context window.
Cached tokens are excluded from the window, so the error must come from an unrelated bug in how the client is assembling each request.
The cache breakpoint is in the wrong place; moving it to the end of the conversation would free up the space currently taken by the history.

questions.explanation: Anthropic's docs are explicit: **cached prompt prefixes still occupy the context window**; prompt caching changes what you pay for those tokens, not whether they count. All three usage fields (`input_tokens`, `cache_read_input_tokens`, `cache_creation_input_tokens`) count toward the window. Long sessions therefore need compaction, clearing old tool results or trimming what is sent.

whyWrong.B: Whether the prefix is cached or not, those tokens count toward the window. Re-caching doesn't free any space.
whyWrong.C: Cached tokens are not excluded, so the conclusion that this must be an unrelated bug is wrong.
whyWrong.D: Moving a breakpoint changes what is reused and billed, not the size of the context.

questions.mindset: Caching saves money and latency, not context space.

questions.stem: A sales-enablement tool generates account briefs. Usage reports show output tokens make up most of the cost, and latency is high. Each brief restates the full input notes, adds a long introduction, and runs far longer than sellers read. The prompt says "Keep it under 300 words", which is often ignored. Which TWO changes MOST effectively reduce output tokens while keeping the briefs useful? Choose TWO.

options.text: Set a much lower max_tokens value so that every brief is forcibly stopped once it reaches the length the sellers actually read.
Tighten the word limit to "under 150 words" and repeat it in capital letters at both the start and end of the prompt.
Specify a fixed structure with sentence or paragraph limits per section, such as three bullet points and a two-sentence next step.
Tell Claude directly to begin with the first section and not to restate the input notes or add an introduction.
Ask Claude to write a full-length draft first and then shorten it in a second paragraph of the same response.

questions.explanation: Anthropic's latency guidance notes that word-count limits are weak because models count tokens, not words; **sentence or paragraph limits** and an explicit structure work better. Direct instructions to drop preamble and restated input remove output the reader never needed. Together they cut output tokens (the cost driver here) and generation time while keeping the brief complete.

whyWrong.A: `max_tokens` is a blunt cap: it truncates mid-sentence rather than producing a shorter, complete brief.
whyWrong.B: A word limit is the type of constraint already being ignored, and capitals don't fix that. Aggressive emphasis can also cause over-correction elsewhere.
whyWrong.E: Draft-then-shorten in one response generates both versions, which increases output tokens and latency.

questions.mindset: Control length with structure and sentence limits, and remove preamble; don't truncate.

questions.stem: An internal IT agent connects to several MCP servers and other integrations exposing about 180 tools. The tool definitions alone take roughly 50,000 tokens on every request, and the agent increasingly picks the wrong tool. Most requests use three to five tools. Which TWO changes BEST reduce context use and improve tool selection? Choose TWO.

options.text: Move every tool definition into the system prompt as plain text so it is cheaper than structured tool definitions sent in the tools array.
Enable the tool search tool and mark rarely used tools with defer_loading, keeping the handful of most frequently used tools loaded up front.
Shorten every tool description to a single sentence so that the full set of 180 definitions takes far fewer tokens on each request.
Switch to a model with a larger context window so the 50,000 tokens of definitions are a smaller fraction of the space available.
Consolidate closely related operations into fewer tools with an action parameter and use consistent service prefixes in tool names.

questions.explanation: Anthropic's tool search docs describe both problems: **context bloat** from loading every definition and **selection accuracy degrading** past roughly 30 to 50 tools. Tool search with `defer_loading` keeps deferred definitions out of context until Claude finds them, and the docs recommend keeping the 3 to 5 most-used tools non-deferred. Tool-definition guidance adds **consolidating related operations** and **meaningful namespacing**, which reduce selection ambiguity and help search match the right tools.

whyWrong.A: The tokens still sit in context on every request, and Claude loses the structured definitions it needs to call the tools correctly.
whyWrong.C: Detailed descriptions are by far the most important factor in tool performance. One-line descriptions would make wrong-tool selection worse.
whyWrong.D: A bigger window doesn't fix selection accuracy, and the 50,000 tokens are still processed and billed on every call.

questions.mindset: Load tools just in time and make the toolset easy to choose from.
